title: The gods choose a human home
hookLine: the gods are offered a cow, then a horse, as a home, and turn both down. then they see a human being
carry: the body is a home for the gods
tomorrow: hunger and thirst ask for a place
last: THE WORLD COMES FROM THE ONE SELF.

lines: THE GODS HAVE NOWHERE TO LIVE.
cards: The worlds are made, and the Aitareya has a house-hunting story. The self shapes a cosmic person and draws the great powers out of it: fire, wind, the sun, the moon. Gods.
But the gods have nowhere to live. They're adrift, the text says, fallen into a great ocean, and they come back asking for a home. So the self brings them a cow.
The gods look it over: no, this isn't enough for us. It brings them a horse. Not enough either.
Then it brings them a human being.

teach.b: When the gods see the person, purusha, they say: sukritam bata. Well made, indeed! That's the Upanishad's verdict on the human body.
Not a prison. Not a burden. A good piece of work, the house the gods accepted.
Then the self says: enter, each into your own place. And no god just walks in. Each one changes shape to fit.

teach.h: FIRE TO SPEECH, SUN TO SIGHT.
teach.b: Fire becomes speech, and enters the mouth. Wind becomes breath, and enters the nostrils. The sun becomes sight, and enters the eyes.
The directions of space become hearing, and enter the ears. Plants and trees become the hairs, and enter the skin. The moon becomes mind, and enters the heart.
Death becomes the down-going breath, and enters the navel. The waters become seed, and enter the organ of generation. When you talk, there's fire in your mouth.
When you look up, the sun is looking out through you. Your changeable mind is the moon.

teach.h: THE BODY: A HOME FOR THE GODS.
teach.b: This is a real thread in Hindu practice: the body as a home for the divine.
In some rites a worshipper touches the limbs one by one while saying mantras, a practice called nyasa, placing the sacred in the body.

It's saying the great powers out there and the small doors in here belong together, and the person is where they meet. So the next time a mirror or a photo tells you your body is a problem, remember the older verdict.
The gods were offered a cow and a horse and said no. They looked at a human being and said: well made, indeed.

how: In Vedic and later Hindu ritual, the body's senses are linked to deities, and some rites include touching the limbs while reciting mantras, a practice called nyasa, which echoes the idea of the gods dwelling in the body.

games.q: who enters which door — tap the pairs.

s: the gods happily moved into the first animal offered
a cow: not enough. a horse: not enough. then a person.
seeing the person, the gods said 'well made, indeed!'
sukritam bata: the text calls the human being well made.
in the story, death has no place in the body
death becomes the down-going breath and enters at the navel.

games.q: a friend says spiritual people should ignore the body: it's just a meat suit. what would the Aitareya say?
o: agree: the body is a prison to escape.
the gods turned down a cow and a horse, chose the person, and called it well made.
only the heart matters; the rest is plumbing.
games.why: sukritam bata: well made, indeed! the gods made the human body their home, fire as speech, sun as sight, the moon as mind.

practice: Bring attention to your closed mouth, where the story puts fire as speech, then to the breath in the nostrils, the wind, and to the eyes, the sun.
Move on to the ears and the directions, the skin and the plants and trees, the heart and the moon as mind. Then rest in the whole house at once, every door open.

wordCard.voice: The person. Purusha, the human being the gods called well made, the one house where fire, wind, sun and moon could each find their door.

orig.note: Sanskrit puruṣa, the person: the human being the gods choose as their home in Aitareya 1.2.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: the body is a home for the gods. Tomorrow, two more guests knock at the door. Four hundred days, done.

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 1.1.3–1.2.4 (the cosmic person; the gods' home; the gods enter the body)
